claim: A domain is a general DNS concept, while a hosted zone is an Amazon Route 53 concept.
question: What is the difference between a domain and a hosted zone?

values.display: hosted zone is an Amazon Route 53 concept

evidence.quote: A domain is a general DNS concept.
A hosted zone is an Amazon Route 53 concept.

claim: A hosted zone is like a traditional DNS zone file: a collection of records that are managed together and belong to one parent domain name.
question: What does a Route 53 hosted zone represent?

evidence.quote: A hosted zone is analogous to a traditional DNS zone file; it represents a collection of records that can be managed together, belonging to a single parent domain name.

claim: All record sets in a hosted zone must have the hosted zone's domain name as a suffix, so the amazon.com zone cannot hold a record named www.amazon.ca.
question: Can a hosted zone for amazon.com hold a record named www.amazon.ca?

evidence.quote: All resource record sets within a hosted zone must have the hosted zone’s domain name as a suffix.
For example, the amazon.com hosted zone may contain records named www.amazon.com, and www.aws.amazon.com, but not a record named www.amazon.ca.

claim: Each Route 53 hosted zone is served by its own set of virtual DNS servers, and the system assigns the DNS server names when the hosted zone is created.
question: Who chooses the DNS server names of a Route 53 hosted zone, and is the set shared between zones?

values.display: its own set of virtual DNS servers

evidence.quote: To provide you with a highly available service, each Amazon Route 53 hosted zone is served by its own set of virtual DNS servers.
The DNS server names for each hosted zone are thus assigned by the system when that hosted zone is created.

claim: When you create a hosted zone you receive four Route 53 name servers across four different top-level domains, to help ensure a high level of availability.
question: How many name servers does Route 53 give you when you create a hosted zone, and across how many TLDs?

qualifiers.condition: on creation of the hosted zone

evidence.quote: Upon creating the hosted zone, you receive four Route 53 name servers across four different Top-Level Domains (TLDs) to help ensure a high level of availability.

claim: You can create multiple hosted zones for the same domain name, for example a test version and a production version, to verify DNS settings before copying them to production.
question: Can you create more than one hosted zone for the same domain name, and why would you?

evidence.quote: Creating multiple hosted zones allows you to verify your DNS setting in a “test” environment, and then replicate those settings on a “production” hosted zone.

claim: Because each hosted zone has its own virtual set of name servers, Route 53 answers queries for the same domain differently depending on which name server receives the query.
question: How does Route 53 keep two hosted zones for the same domain apart?

values.display: depending on which name server you send the DNS query to

qualifiers.scope: hosted zones for the same domain

evidence.quote: Since each hosted zone has a virtual set of name servers associated with that zone, Route 53 will answer DNS queries for example.com differently depending on which name server you send the DNS query to.

claim: The FAQ states that each Route 53 account is limited to a maximum of 500 hosted zones, and that a higher limit can be requested.
question: What is the maximum number of hosted zones per Route 53 account according to the FAQ?

qualifiers.condition: a higher limit can be requested

evidence.quote: Each Amazon Route 53 account is limited to a maximum of 500 hosted zones and 10,000 resource record sets per hosted zone.
Complete our request for a higher limit and we will respond to your request within two business days.

claim: The FAQ states that each hosted zone is limited to a maximum of 10,000 resource record sets, and that a higher limit can be requested.
question: What is the maximum number of resource record sets per hosted zone according to the FAQ?

qualifiers.condition: a higher limit can be requested

evidence.quote: Each Amazon Route 53 account is limited to a maximum of 500 hosted zones and 10,000 resource record sets per hosted zone.
Complete our request for a higher limit and we will respond to your request within two business days.

claim: Route 53 does not provide website hosting because it is an authoritative DNS service; use Amazon S3 for a static website and Amazon EC2 for a dynamic website.
question: Does Route 53 host websites?

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 is an authoritative DNS service and does not provide website hosting.
However, you can use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) to host a static website.

claim: An alias record usually has the type A or AAAA but works like a CNAME record.
question: What record type does a Route 53 alias record have, and what does it work like?

evidence.quote: Alias record typically have a type of A or AAAA, but they work like a CNAME record.

claim: Alias records are an Amazon Route 53-specific extension to DNS, used to route traffic to selected AWS resources.
question: Are alias records part of standard DNS?

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 also offers alias records, which are an Amazon Route 53-specific extension to DNS.

claim: Alias records can route traffic to Elastic Load Balancing load balancers, CloudFront distributions, Elastic Beanstalk environments, API Gateways, VPC interface endpoints and S3 buckets that are configured as websites.
question: Which AWS resources can a Route 53 alias record point to, according to the FAQ?

values.display: S3 buckets that are configured as websites

qualifiers.condition: list as stated in the FAQ

evidence.quote: You can create alias records to route traffic to selected AWS resources, including Amazon Elastic Load Balancing load balancers, Amazon CloudFront distributions, AWS Elastic Beanstalk environments, API Gateways, VPC interface endpoints, and Amazon S3 buckets that are configured as websites.

claim: Alias records can map sub-domains such as www.example.com to ELB load balancers, CloudFront distributions or S3 website buckets.
question: Can alias records be used for sub-domains, and for which targets?

evidence.quote: You can also use Alias records to map your sub-domains (www.example.com, pictures.example.com, etc.) to your ELB load balancers, CloudFront distributions, or S3 website buckets.

claim: Route 53 supports wildcard entries for all record types except NS records.
question: Which record types support wildcard entries in Route 53?

values.display: all record types, except NS records

evidence.quote: To make it even easier for you to configure DNS settings for your domain, Amazon Route 53 supports wildcard entries for all record types, except NS records.

claim: A wildcard record such as *.example.com matches queries for names like www.example.com and subdomain.example.com.
question: What does the wildcard record *.example.com match?

evidence.quote: For example, a wildcard DNS record such as *.example.com will match queries for www.example.com and subdomain.example.com.

claim: Route 53 has no default TTL for any record type, so you must always specify a TTL for each record.
question: What is the default TTL for Route 53 records?

values.display: does not have a default TTL

qualifiers.condition: a TTL must be set on each record

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 does not have a default TTL for any record type.
You must always specify a TTL for each record so that caching DNS resolvers can cache your DNS records to the length of time specified through the TTL.

claim: Route 53 changes to record sets are transactional: a change completes entirely on any individual DNS server, or not at all.
question: Are changes to Route 53 resource record sets transactional?

values.display: complete entirely on any individual DNS server, or not at all

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 has been designed so that changes complete entirely on any individual DNS server, or not at all.

claim: When the status of a change is INSYNC, the change has been performed on all of the Route 53 DNS servers.
question: What does the INSYNC status of a Route 53 change mean?

evidence.quote: Once the status is reported as INSYNC, your change has been performed on all of the Route 53 DNS servers.

claim: Route 53 is designed to propagate record updates to its world-wide authoritative DNS servers within 60 seconds under normal conditions.
question: How quickly does Route 53 propagate DNS record changes to its authoritative servers?

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 is designed to propagate updates you make to your DNS records to its world-wide network of authoritative DNS servers within 60 seconds under normal conditions.

claim: Caching DNS resolvers are outside the control of Route 53 and cache record sets according to their TTL, so INSYNC or PENDING describes only the state of Route 53's authoritative servers.
question: Why can a client still see an old DNS value after Route 53 reports a change as INSYNC?

values.display: according to their time to live (TTL)

evidence.quote: Note that caching DNS resolvers are outside the control of the Amazon Route 53 service and will cache your resource record sets according to their time to live (TTL).
The INSYNC or PENDING status of a change refers only to the state of Route 53’s authoritative DNS servers.
